title: Chemical Equilibrium

notes.heading: 1. Law of Mass Action, Kp vs Kc & Equilibrium Constant Algebra
notes.proseLatex: For $aA + bB \rightleftharpoons cC + dD$, pure solids and pure liquids have unit activity and are OMITTED from $K_c$ and $K_p$ (e.g., $\text{CaCO}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)$ has $K_p = p_{\text{CO}_2}$!). Ideal gases satisfy $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$ where $\Delta n_g = (c+d) - (a+b)$ counts ONLY gaseous moles. Reversing a reaction inverts $K' = 1/K$, multiplying stoichiometry by $m$ raises $K' = K^m$, and adding two equilibria multiplies $K_{\text{net}} = K_1 K_2$.

keyFormulas.label: Kp–Kc Relation & Stoichiometric Scaling Rules
keyFormulas.latex: $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g},\qquad \text{reverse}: K' = \frac{1}{K},\qquad \times m: K' = K^m$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Relate Kp and Kc (watch gaseous moles only!) and combine multi-step equilibrium constants.

notes.heading: 2. Reaction Quotient Qc, Le Chatelier's Principle & Inert-Gas Addition
notes.proseLatex: Comparing $Q_c$ to $K_c$: $Q_c < K_c$ drives forward reaction, $Q_c > K_c$ drives reverse. Increasing total pressure (decreasing volume) shifts equilibrium toward FEWER gas moles ($\Delta n_g$ side). Raising temperature shifts toward the ENDOTHERMIC direction (and is the ONLY disturbance that changes the numerical value of $K$, via van 't Hoff $\ln\frac{K_2}{K_1} = \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)$). Adding inert gas at CONSTANT VOLUME changes no partial pressures so equilibrium does NOT shift; at CONSTANT PRESSURE it increases volume and shifts toward MORE gas moles!

keyFormulas.label: van 't Hoff Temperature Dependence of K
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Predict temperature, pressure, catalyst, and inert-gas effects on equilibrium.

notes.heading: 3. Haber (NH₃) & Contact (SO₃) Industrial Equilibria
notes.proseLatex: Both Haber's ammonia synthesis ($\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3,\; \Delta H < 0,\; \Delta n_g = -2$) and Contact $\text{SO}_3$ oxidation ($2\text{SO}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SO}_3,\; \Delta H < 0,\; \Delta n_g = -1$) are exothermic mole-decreasing reactions: high pressure favours yield thermodynamically, while an optimum moderate temperature ($\sim 700\text{ K}$) plus catalyst ($\text{Fe}$ with $\text{Mo}/\text{K}_2\text{O}$ promoter in Haber; $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ in Contact) balances kinetic rate without destroying $K$.

keyFormulas.label: Haber & Contact Process Conditions
keyFormulas.latex: $\text{Haber: Fe catalyst, }200\text{ atm, }\sim 700\text{ K};\qquad \text{Contact: V}_2\text{O}_5\text{ catalyst, }1\text{--}2\text{ atm, }\sim 720\text{ K}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Recall industrial catalysts and why moderate T rather than 0 C is used.

wbjeebTraps: A catalyst speeds up forward and reverse rates EQUALLY — it cuts time to reach equilibrium but NEVER changes $K_c$, $K_p$, or equilibrium yield!
Adding inert gas at CONSTANT VOLUME produces ZERO shift for every reaction; only CONSTANT-PRESSURE inert-gas addition shifts toward higher gas moles (when $\Delta n_g \neq 0$).
Count ONLY gaseous species in $\Delta n_g$: for $\text{C}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{CO}(g)$, $\Delta n_g = 2 - 1 = +1$ (ignore solid carbon!).
